title: 2025 APM Measurement Effort (CY2024 data): about 45% of payments in APMs
questions: What share of U.S. health care payments flow through alternative payment models?
What did the latest HCP-LAN / AHIP APM Measurement Effort find?
How much of Medicare Advantage spending is in value-based contracts?
Is APM adoption still growing or has it plateaued?
summary: The 2025 APM Measurement Effort, run by AHIP after it took over the HCP-LAN survey in the second half of 2025 and released in early 2026, covers calendar year 2024. About 44.9% of U.S. health care payments across all lines of business flowed through Category 3-4 APMs, essentially flat versus 45.2% the prior year, and roughly 28.7% went through downside-risk contracts. Medicare Advantage remained the most advanced line of business (60.0% in Categories 3-4 and about 45% with downside risk), followed by Traditional Medicare (44.4%), Medicaid (42.7%) and commercial (38.9%, down slightly from 39.2%). About 40% of payments were still pure fee-for-service with no link to quality. The survey covered 58 health plans, two fee-for-service Medicaid states and Traditional Medicare, representing over 271 million people. The headline story is a plateau: after steady gains from 2015 to 2023, the APM share stopped rising in 2024 and MA's share fell about four points.

title: 2024 APM Measurement Effort (CY2023 data): 28.5% of payments in downside-risk APMs
questions: How much health care spending was in two-sided risk models in 2023?
What share of Traditional Medicare beneficiaries were in accountable care in 2023?

summary: HCP-LAN's 2024 Measurement Effort reported calendar-year 2023 payments. Across all lines of business, 28.5% of U.S. health care payments flowed through downside-risk contracts (Categories 3B and 4), 16.7% through upside-only shared savings (3A), and 54.8% remained in Categories 1-2, implying about 45.2% in Categories 3-4. Medicare Advantage led on downside risk (43%, mostly Category 4 population-based payment at 34%), followed by Traditional Medicare (33.7%), commercial (21.6%) and Medicaid (21.1%). The LAN also began counting lives in accountable care arrangements: 88.5 million lives reported by respondents, including 49.5% of eligible Traditional Medicare beneficiaries (14.1 million of 28.4 million) and 29.1% of Medicaid lives reported. Payers were optimistic: 76% expected APM activity to increase and none expected a decrease.

summary: HCP-LAN's 2023 Measurement Effort (calendar-year 2022 payments) found 24.5% of U.S. health care payments flowing through two-sided risk contracts (Categories 3B-4) across all lines of business, with 16.7% in upside-only Category 3A and 58.7% in Categories 1-2, implying roughly 41.3% in Categories 3-4 overall. By line of business, two-sided risk reached 38.9% in Medicare Advantage, 30.2% in Traditional Medicare, 18.7% in Medicaid and 16.5% in commercial. Commercial payers were the laggard, with 65.4% of payments still in Categories 1-2 and only 4.1% in population-based Category 4 payments, compared with 24.6% Category 4 in Medicare Advantage. These figures are the baseline for the year-over-year jump to 28.5% downside risk in 2023.

summary: HCP-LAN's 2022 Measurement Effort, based on 63 plans, 5 states and Traditional Medicare, found that in calendar year 2021 only 19.6% of U.S. health care payments flowed through two-sided risk models (Categories 3B-4). The aggregate breakdown was about 40.5% pure fee-for-service, 19.5% fee-for-service linked to quality, 20.4% upside-only shared savings (3A), 12.2% shared savings with downside risk (3B) and 7.4% population-based payment (Category 4), so roughly 40% sat in Categories 3-4. Two-sided risk was highest in Medicare Advantage (35.2%) and Traditional Medicare (24.0%), lower in Medicaid (16.6%) and lowest in commercial (12.7%). This is the snapshot the LAN used when it reset its goals toward 2030.

title: APM adoption trend 2021-2024: steady growth in downside risk, then a plateau
questions: Is value-based payment adoption accelerating?
How has the share of payments in APMs changed since 2021?
Has downside risk adoption stalled?
summary: Lining up four consecutive HCP-LAN/AHIP measurement efforts shows the arc of APM adoption. The share of payments in Categories 3-4 rose from about 40% (2021) to 41.3% (2022) and 45.2% (2023), then held at 44.9% in 2024. Downside-risk adoption (Categories 3B-4) grew faster, from 19.6% to 24.5%, 28.5% and about 28.7%. Most of the earlier gain came from Medicare Advantage and Traditional Medicare; commercial two-sided risk rose from 12.7% to 21.6% between 2021 and 2023 but the commercial Category 3-4 share slipped slightly in 2024. The overall pattern is rapid growth through 2023 followed by a flattening, leaving all lines of business behind the LAN's interim 2025 goals. Note that the respondent pool changes each year, so year-to-year shifts partly reflect sample composition.

title: HCP-LAN 2030 APM goals by line of business
questions: What are the HCP-LAN 2030 goals for value-based payment?
What is the 2030 goal for accountable care in Medicare?
What share of commercial payments should be in downside risk by 2030?
summary: After the pandemic, the LAN reset its alternative payment model goals to 2030 and redefined success as two-sided risk only (Categories 3B and 4). Its targets are 100% of Medicare Advantage and Original Medicare payments, and 50% of commercial and Medicaid payments, in Categories 3B-4 by 2030, with interim goals of 25%/25%/55%/50% (Medicaid/commercial/MA/Original Medicare) in 2024 and 30%/30%/65%/60% in 2025. The goals are explicitly tied to CMS's 2021 aim of having all Medicare beneficiaries and the vast majority of Medicaid beneficiaries in an accountable relationship by 2030; the LAN reads 'vast majority' as about 75% of Medicaid beneficiaries. The document also adopted a formal definition of accountable care and an 'Accountable Care Curve' with measurement tracks for payment reform, quality, data and infrastructure, and multi-stakeholder alignment, stressing that payment is only one enabler. It cites barriers such as stagnant MSSP enrollment despite Pathways to Success and limited leverage of small commercial payers.

title: Progress against HCP-LAN interim goals: every line of business behind
questions: Are payers on track to meet the 2030 APM goals?
How far is Medicare Advantage from the HCP-LAN downside risk target?

summary: Comparing the LAN's interim Category 3B-4 goals with measured adoption shows every line of business behind schedule. The 2024 goal for Medicare Advantage was 55% in two-sided risk; measured 2024 MA downside-risk share was about 45%. For Original Medicare the 2024 goal was 50%, versus 33.7% in 2023, the latest year with a published Traditional Medicare 3B-4 figure. Commercial (goal 25%) measured 21.6% and Medicaid (goal 25%) 21.1% in 2023. With all-payer downside-risk adoption roughly flat between 2023 (28.5%) and 2024 (about 28.7%), the 2025 interim goals (65% MA, 60% Original Medicare, 30% commercial and Medicaid) look out of reach on the measured trajectory. This is an analytic comparison of LAN goals and LAN/AHIP survey data, not a LAN-published scorecard.

title: Health Care Transformation Task Force critique of the LAN 2030 goals
questions: Who criticized the HCP-LAN 2030 APM goals and why?
Is 100% downside risk in Medicare by 2030 realistic?
What is the Health Care Transformation Task Force's value-based care goal?
summary: In February 2023 the Health Care Transformation Task Force, a payer-provider-purchaser consortium, responded to the LAN's draft 2030 goals. It accepted pushing the Medicare deadline to 2030 as reflecting market reality, noting that its own members' target of 75% of business in value-based models had already slipped from 2020 to 2025. But it argued the 50% goals for commercial and Medicaid were too weak to accelerate those markets, and that requiring 100% of Medicare in downside-risk models by 2030 may be unrealistic. The Task Force counts all of Categories 3 and 4, including upside-only arrangements, and noted that CMS itself had softened Pathways to Success in 2023 rulemaking by making the Enhanced track optional and allowing new ACOs up to seven years upside-only. It supported a longer glide path to mandatory risk, especially for safety-net providers.

title: HCP-LAN APM Framework categories (1, 2, 3A/3B, 4A/4B/4C)
questions: What are the HCP-LAN APM Framework categories?
What is the difference between Category 3A and 3B?
What counts as Category 4 population-based payment?
summary: The HCP-LAN APM Framework sorts payments into four categories, and its measurement reports use subcategories. Category 1 is fee-for-service with no link to quality or value. Category 2 is fee-for-service linked to quality and value: foundational infrastructure payments, pay-for-reporting and pay-for-performance. Category 3 covers APMs built on fee-for-service architecture: 3A gives upside-only rewards (shared savings), while 3B adds downside risk, such as episode payments or shared savings with losses. Category 4 is prospective population-based payment: 4A is condition-specific, 4B is comprehensive, and 4C is an integrated finance and delivery system. The LAN's 2030 goals count only Categories 3B and 4, so an MSSP ACO in an upside-only BASIC level would be Category 3A, while a two-sided ACO counts as 3B. In CY2021 data, Category 4 made up 7.4% of payments (4A 2.1%, 4B 4.5%, 4C 0.8%).

categories.2: FFS linked to quality/value (2A foundational, 2B pay-for-reporting, 2C pay-for-performance)
categories.3B: APM on FFS architecture, upside and downside

title: MSSP at January 2026: 511 ACOs, 12.6 million assigned beneficiaries
questions: How many ACOs are in the Medicare Shared Savings Program in 2026?
How many beneficiaries are assigned to MSSP ACOs?
What share of MSSP ACOs take downside risk?
How many clinicians participate in MSSP?
summary: CMS's Shared Savings Program Fast Facts for January 1, 2026 show the program at its largest beneficiary count yet: 511 ACOs with 12.6 million assigned beneficiaries, up from 476 ACOs and 11.2 million in 2025. About 76% of ACOs are in two-sided risk (58% ENHANCED, 16% BASIC level E, 2% levels C-D) and 24% remain one-sided (BASIC A-B), compared with 71% two-sided a year earlier. Participant lists include 15,353 TINs, 687,739 physicians and non-physician practitioners, 1,539 hospitals, 8,840 FQHCs, 3,109 rural health clinics and 590 critical access hospitals. Low-revenue ACOs (typically physician-led) are 64% of the program. Assigned beneficiaries are about 87.7% aged non-dual, 6.6% disabled, 5.3% aged dual and under 1% ESRD. 183 ACOs hold a SNF 3-day rule waiver. Note that Fast Facts counts are as of January 1 and differ from performance-year reconciliation counts.

title: MSSP ACO counts and assigned beneficiaries, 2012-2026
questions: How has the number of MSSP ACOs changed over time?
When did MSSP participation peak?
Did ACO participation decline after Pathways to Success?
summary: CMS Fast Facts give the MSSP's size at the start of each year. The program grew from 220 ACOs (3.2 million beneficiaries) in its 2012-2013 launch cohort to a peak of 561 ACOs in 2018 (10.5 million). After the 2018 Pathways to Success rule shortened the upside-only period and cut shared savings rates, the count fell to 487 in 2019, rebounded briefly to 517 in 2020, then dropped to 477 in 2021 and hovered at 456-483 through 2025. Beneficiary counts held steadier, between about 10.4 and 11.2 million from 2019 to 2025, because surviving ACOs grew larger. In 2026 the program reached 511 ACOs and a record 12.6 million beneficiaries. The ACO count has still not returned to the 2018 high, which NAACOS attributes to the Pathways policies.

title: MSSP total earned shared savings by performance year

summary: CMS Fast Facts report total shared savings earned by MSSP ACOs for each performance year. Payments rose from $315 million for the 2012-2013 cohort to $341 million (2014), $645 million (2015), $700 million (2016), $799 million (2017), $983 million (2018), $1.5 billion (2019), $2.3 billion (2020), $2.0 billion (2021), $2.5 billion (2022), $3.1 billion (2023) and $4.1 billion (2024). These are payments to ACOs, not net Medicare savings; net savings to Medicare are reported separately (for example $2.5 billion in 2024). Average quality scores fell from the low-to-mid 90s to about 81-82% from 2022 onward, which CMS attributes to elimination of MIPS bonus points rather than worse care.

title: MSSP Performance Year 2024 results: $4.1B to ACOs, $2.5B saved for Medicare
questions: How much did Medicare save from ACOs in 2024?
What were MSSP 2024 financial results?
How many ACOs earned shared savings in 2024?
How many ACOs owed losses in 2024?
summary: CMS's updated fact sheet (September 29, 2025) reports the best year in MSSP history. Of 476 ACOs, 75%, covering 80% of 10.3 million assigned beneficiaries, earned performance payments totaling $4.1 billion, and Medicare saved $2.5 billion relative to benchmarks. Net per capita savings (Medicare's share) rose to $245 from $207 in 2023, and gross per capita savings to $651 from $515. Sixteen ACOs owed shared losses totaling $20.0 million. ACOs that earned savings had lower utilization than benchmark in hospital discharges, ED visits and SNF stays. Savings are measured against administratively set benchmarks, so they depend on benchmark design and are not the same as savings versus a counterfactual comparison group. CMS paired the results with proposals to shorten one-sided participation to five years.

title: Physician-led (low-revenue) ACOs outperform hospital-led ACOs
questions: Do physician-led ACOs save more than hospital-led ACOs?
What is a low revenue ACO?
Do primary-care-heavy ACOs perform better?
summary: CMS distinguishes low-revenue ACOs, typically physician-led groups or FQHC/RHC-based ACOs, from high-revenue ACOs, which are usually hospital-led. In performance year 2024, low-revenue ACOs generated $319 in net per capita savings for Medicare versus $180 for high-revenue ACOs. ACOs made up predominantly of primary care clinicians did better still, $403 versus $224 net per capita for ACOs with fewer primary care clinicians. CMS describes this as a continuing pattern. Low-revenue ACOs are also the majority of the program: 325 of 511 ACOs (64%) in January 2026. NAACOS and others have pushed to eliminate the high/low revenue distinction in law, arguing it is used to treat ACOs differently for eligibility and track rules rather than reflecting performance.

title: NAACOS on falling MSSP participation after Pathways to Success (2021)
questions: Why did ACO participation decline after 2018?
What is NAACOS's view of Pathways to Success?
What did NAACOS ask the Biden administration to change in MSSP?
summary: In January 2021 NAACOS warned that MSSP participation had fallen to 477 ACOs, down from 561 in 2018 and the lowest since 2017, though they still served 10.7 million beneficiaries. It blamed the 2018 Pathways to Success rule, which cut the basic shared savings rate from 50% to 40% and shrank the no-risk runway from six years to as little as two, plus CMS's cancellation of 2021 applications during the pandemic. NAACOS argued that equating risk with value is a mistake, that providers should succeed under one-sided models before taking losses, and that forcing risk could push providers back to uncoordinated fee-for-service. Its asks included reopening applications, raising shared savings rates, fixing benchmarking and risk adjustment, more time before mandatory risk, making the Enhanced track voluntary, better data and less administrative burden. CMS later made the Enhanced track optional and extended upside-only time in its CY2023 rule.

title: NAACOS on the benchmark ratchet and the ACPT
questions: What is the ratchet effect in ACO benchmarks?
Why does NAACOS oppose the ACPT?
What benchmark changes does NAACOS want from Congress?
summary: NAACOS argues that MSSP benchmarks 'ratchet' down: because each new agreement period rebases on the ACO's own recent spending, ACOs that lower costs get lower targets and progressively less room to earn savings, which threatens long-term participation. Its 2024 one-pager says MSSP has produced more than $21 billion in gross savings but CMS has not addressed the ratchet. It criticizes CMS's Accountable Care Prospective Trend (ACPT), a fixed national growth projection added to benchmark updates, because a national trend does not match local spending and penalizes ACOs in slow-growth regions; it cites CMS analysis that ACPT would harm nearly one third of ACOs. NAACOS asks Congress for transparent, replicable benchmarks, a fix to the ratchet, an appeals and third-party review process, regional adjustments set as if the ACO were not in its market, and study of payment differences between ACOs and Medicare Advantage.

title: Ways and Means testimony: a long-running ACO expects to exit because of the ratchet (2024)
questions: Why would a successful ACO leave MSSP?
How does the benchmark ratchet affect a mature ACO?
How do MSSP benchmarks compare with Medicare Advantage risk contracts for providers?
summary: Stephen Nuckolls, CEO of Coastal Carolina Quality Care and a NAACOS board member, testified to the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee in June 2024. His ACO, an original 2012 MSSP entrant, reports spending $84 million below benchmark since joining, netting Medicare $28 million, and cutting hospitalizations 39% and ED visits 28%. Its cost per patient is now about 25% below its region. Because rebasing will cut its benchmark by roughly 10 percentage points even after the 5% cap on the prior savings or regional efficiency adjustment, he said the ACO was unlikely to renew. He contrasted this with the ACO's Medicare Advantage risk contracts, which do not ratchet and are more predictable. He urged sustainable benchmarks, extension of the advanced APM incentive, incentives across the care continuum, and less regulatory burden. This is one ACO's self-reported experience, presented as advocacy.

title: NAACOS cumulative ACO savings claims and how they compare with CMS figures

summary: NAACOS regularly cites cumulative savings to argue ACOs are a good federal investment, and the figures have grown over time. In early 2022 it cited $13.3 billion in gross savings and $4.7 billion net. Its 2024 benchmark one-pager cites more than $21 billion in gross savings, and its June 2024 Ways and Means testimony cites more than $22.4 billion in savings over the past decade with $8.8 billion returned to the Medicare Trust Fund. For PY2020 alone it reported $4.1 billion gross and $1.9 billion net. The key distinction is gross savings (total spending below benchmark, shared between ACOs and Medicare) versus net savings (what Medicare keeps after shared savings payments). All are measured against administrative benchmarks rather than a comparison group. NAACOS figures are advocacy summaries of CMS data.

title: NAACOS 2022 MSSP enhancement asks: rural glitch, risk caps, 50% savings rate
questions: What is the ACO rural glitch?
What changes did NAACOS ask CMS to make to MSSP in 2022?
What risk adjustment cap does NAACOS want for ACOs?
summary: In a March 2022 letter to CMS, NAACOS laid out a long list of MSSP fixes. On benchmarks, it asked CMS to fix the 'rural glitch' by removing an ACO's own assigned beneficiaries from its regional comparison, citing Institute for Accountable Care research that 90% of MSSP ACOs would benefit; to widen the risk-score cap to plus or minus 5% (noting the existing 3% cap would have bound 87% of ACOs in their first three years using PY2017 data); to cap ACO and regional risk consistently; and to use a regional-only trend. It also sought at least a 50% shared savings rate, at least four years before mandatory risk, an optional Enhanced track, a full-risk 'Enhanced Plus' option with 100% sharing, elimination of the high/low revenue distinction, deeming all MSSP ACOs Advanced APMs, extended APM incentives, better data access (ADT alerts), and quality scoring decoupled from MIPS, warning CMS estimated about 20% of ACOs would fail the new quality standard.

title: NAACOS January 2024 MSSP recommendations: fix the ratchet, raise the 5% cap, Enhanced Plus
questions: What did NAACOS recommend to CMS in 2024?
How does NAACOS want the prior savings adjustment changed?
What is the proposed MSSP Enhanced Plus track?
summary: NAACOS's January 2024 recommendations to CMS centered on the fiscal reality of staying in APMs. It asked CMS to correct the benchmark ratchet; to enlarge the prior savings adjustment (pay 50% of the average regional adjustment plus 100% of savings above it) and let it exceed the current 5% cap; to risk-adjust any caps; to credit savings older than three years; to stop penalizing ACOs that spend above their region; to fix the rural glitch; and to base trends on the ACO's region rather than a national rate, adding guardrails to the ACPT. On quality, it asked to keep the Medicare CQM option until digital measures are feasible and to oppose mandatory MVPs. It proposed an 'Enhanced Plus' track offering full risk with a 2-3% discount or 85-90% shared savings, NPI-level participation and population-based payments, plus a high-needs track and broader waivers.

title: Value in Health Care Act: the ACO community's legislative package
questions: What is the Value in Health Care Act?
What legislation does NAACOS support?

summary: The Value in Health Care Act, introduced in several Congresses with bipartisan House sponsors, is the main legislative vehicle backed by NAACOS, AMA and other groups. Versions have proposed restoring higher MSSP shared savings rates, modifying risk adjustment, ending the high/low revenue ACO labels, removing ACO beneficiaries from the regional benchmark (the rural glitch fix), restarting the ACO Investment Model, extending the 5% Advanced APM incentive payment, studying overlap among Medicare APMs, and commissioning a GAO report on outcomes and disparities. A NAACOS-commissioned Moran Company analysis estimated about $280 million in savings over 10 years (an advocacy-commissioned estimate, not a CBO score). In 2024 NAACOS testified for H.R. 5013, which would extend the original advanced APM incentive and freeze qualifying thresholds for 2025-2026.

How many clinicians are in advanced APMs?
summary: MACRA (2015) created a lump-sum incentive for clinicians who qualify through Advanced APMs, originally 5% of Part B professional payments; Congress has passed short-term extensions. NAACOS testimony in 2024 credited the incentive with helping more than 400,000 clinicians move into Advanced APMs and with more than 70% of the 602 MSSP and REACH ACOs taking two-sided risk by January 2024. One ACO reported receiving $600,000-700,000 a year, about 5-10% of its shared savings and under 1% of its benchmark, and said it gave clinicians confidence to accept downside risk and offset inflation. NAACOS argued that once incentives lapse, MIPS bonuses can rival APM rewards, weakening the business case, and asked for timely payment (there is a two-year lag) and for higher APM conversion-factor updates not to count against benchmarks.

title: How ACO shared savings are used inside physician organizations
questions: How do ACO shared savings get distributed to doctors?
What do ACOs spend their shared savings on?
Do specialists benefit from ACO savings?
summary: MSSP pays shared savings to the ACO entity, not to individual clinicians, so the ACO decides how dollars flow internally. NAACOS testimony describes common uses: expanding care teams, paying for services Medicare does not bill, enhanced clinician compensation for retention, and investment in technology and care coordination. One independent multispecialty ACO said it uses savings to subsidize specialists such as cardiologists so their pay stays competitive with hospital-employed peers, and that savings plus APM incentives offset annual losses to inflation. The same testimony argues that specialists and other providers outside primary care still face fee-for-service incentives, so ACOs need ways to bring them in. Distribution methods vary widely and are not standardized or publicly reported.

title: How MSSP benchmarks are set (MedPAC summary)
questions: How is an MSSP ACO's benchmark calculated?
What is the prior savings adjustment?
How does MSSP cap risk score growth?
Why do regional and historical benchmarks matter?
summary: MedPAC's payment basics explain that an MSSP benchmark starts with the Part A and B spending of beneficiaries who would have been assigned to the ACO in the three years before its agreement, weighted toward the most recent year. That historical baseline is blended with average regional fee-for-service spending for assignable beneficiaries in the ACO's market. From 2024, a prior-savings adjustment can raise the baseline to credit some savings generated in the prior three years; if it exceeds the regional-blend result, the ACO gets historical spending plus that adjustment. From 2025 the benchmark is also adjusted for the share of low-income beneficiaries. The baseline is trended forward with a three-way blend of a fixed projected growth rate (the ACPT) and actual regional and national FFS growth. Risk scores use HCCs, are normalized for coding changes across all assignable FFS beneficiaries, and an ACO's risk score growth is capped at 3 percentage points above demographic change.

facts.trend: three-way blend: ACPT (fixed projection), regional, national FFS growth

title: MSSP track and level parameters: shared savings and loss rates
questions: What shared savings rate do MSSP ACOs get?
What is the difference between BASIC and ENHANCED tracks?
How much downside risk does MSSP Level E carry?
summary: Per MedPAC's 2025 summary of CMS rules, BASIC levels A and B are upside-only with a 40% maximum shared savings rate capped at 10% of benchmark. Levels C, D and E offer 50% savings (capped at 10% of benchmark) and a 30% shared loss rate, with loss caps of 2% of revenue or 1% of benchmark (C), 4% of revenue or 2% of benchmark (D), and 8% of revenue or 4% of benchmark (E), whichever is lower; Level E meets Advanced APM requirements. The ENHANCED track pays up to 75% of savings, capped at 20% of benchmark, with a 40-75% loss rate that falls as quality rises, capped at 15% of benchmark. Higher quality reduces the loss rate in two-sided arrangements, and ACOs must meet a minimum quality standard to earn savings. These rates are the subject of NAACOS's push to raise BASIC shared savings rates.

title: CY2024 rule: ACPT added, negative regional adjustment eliminated, regional risk cap
questions: What is the ACPT in MSSP?
Did CMS remove the negative regional adjustment for ACOs?
What benchmark changes took effect for ACOs in 2024?
summary: CMS's CY2024 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (November 2, 2023) reworked MSSP benchmark updates for agreement periods starting January 1, 2024 or later. It added the Accountable Care Prospective Trend (ACPT), a growth rate fixed in advance for the agreement period, as one third of a three-way blended update factor alongside regional and national trends. It eliminated the overall negative regional adjustment, so ACOs that spend more than their region are no longer penalized through the regional blend. It also capped prospective HCC risk score growth in an ACO's regional service area, mirroring the ACO-level cap and accounting for market share. NAACOS welcomed some changes but warned the ACPT's national basis would hurt ACOs in slower-growing regions, citing CMS analysis that nearly a third would be harmed.

title: MedPAC 2025: MA paid ~20% ($84B) more than FFS, driven by coding and selection
questions: How much more does Medicare pay MA plans than traditional Medicare?
What is MA coding intensity?
How big is favorable selection in Medicare Advantage?
Why does MA coding matter for ACOs?
summary: MedPAC's March 2025 status report estimates Medicare will pay MA plans about $84 billion (about 20%) more in 2025 than if enrollees were in fee-for-service. Two drivers dominate. Coding intensity: MA risk scores were about 17% higher than for similar FFS beneficiaries in 2023 and are projected about 16% higher in 2025; after CMS's statutory minimum 5.9% reduction, they remain about 10% higher, worth roughly $40 billion. Favorable selection: MA enrollees cost less than their risk scores predict, adding about 11% ($44 billion). Coding varies widely: 16 MA organizations code more than 20% above FFS, and the ten largest differ by 26 points. About half of excess coding traces to chart reviews and health risk assessments. For ACO analytics, the relevance is indirect: MSSP benchmarks are built from FFS spending and FFS-calibrated risk models, while providers in MA risk contracts face different coding incentives.

title: KFF 2026: Medicare Advantage covers 55% of eligible beneficiaries
questions: What share of Medicare beneficiaries are in Medicare Advantage?
How many people are enrolled in MA in 2026?
Is Medicare Advantage growth slowing?
What does CBO project for MA enrollment?
summary: KFF's June 2026 enrollment update counts 35.2 million Medicare Advantage enrollees out of 64.2 million eligible beneficiaries with Parts A and B, or 55%, up from 19% in 2007. Growth is slowing: enrollment rose about 1.1 million (3%) from 2025, after 4% the prior year. Special needs plans now hold 23% of MA enrollment (about 8.2 million) and accounted for 85% of the net increase, with chronic-condition SNPs growing fastest. CBO projects MA's share will reach 63% by 2034. For ACO and VBC analysis, MA's majority share means traditional Medicare, where MSSP and REACH operate, is now the smaller part of Medicare, and the FFS population used to set ACO regional benchmarks is shaped by who stays out of MA.

title: When Medicare Advantage passed 50% of eligible beneficiaries
questions: When did Medicare Advantage enroll more than half of Medicare beneficiaries?

summary: In August 2022 KFF reported that 28.4 million of 58.6 million eligible beneficiaries (48%) were in Medicare Advantage and projected that MA would pass 50% in 2023, becoming the predominant way people with Parts A and B get Medicare. KFF's 2026 update confirms MA enrollment has been above half of eligible beneficiaries since 2023. KFF also changed its method at that time to count only beneficiaries with both Part A and Part B as eligible, which yields a somewhat higher share than older methods. MedPAC put 2024 enrollment at 33.6 million (54%), and KFF's 2025 figure was also 54%, before reaching 55% in 2026. title: Medicare Advantage market concentration: UnitedHealth and Humana hold 46%
questions: Which companies dominate Medicare Advantage?
What is UnitedHealthcare's share of MA enrollment?
How concentrated is the MA market?
summary: KFF's 2026 data show UnitedHealth Group and Humana together enroll 46% of all Medicare Advantage members, the same combined share as 2025, but the mix shifted: UnitedHealth fell to 26% (9.3 million) from 29% after losing about 647,000 enrollees, while Humana rose to 20% (7.0 million) from 17% after gaining about 1.3 million. CVS Health (Aetna) holds 12%, Kaiser Foundation Health Plan 6% and Elevance Health 5%. In 2025, by contrast, UnitedHealth had gained about 505,000 members and Humana lost about 297,000, showing how quickly plan exits and benefit changes move members. Concentration matters for providers because a few payers set most MA value-based contract terms in many markets.

title: ACO REACH (and GPDC) participation and savings, 2021-2026
questions: How many ACOs are in ACO REACH?
How many beneficiaries are aligned to REACH ACOs?
How much has ACO REACH saved?
Is ACO REACH shrinking?
summary: CMS's PY2026 participant notice includes model fast facts for ACO REACH and its predecessor, Global and Professional Direct Contracting. Participation rose from 53 ACOs (354,333 aligned beneficiaries) in 2021 to 99 in 2022 (1.8 million) and a peak of 132 in 2023 (2.0 million), then fell to 122 in 2024 (2.6 million), 103 in 2025 (2.5 million) and 74 in 2026 (1.7 million beneficiaries, 125,909 providers). In 2026, 65 ACOs chose Global risk (100% of savings and losses) and 9 chose Professional (50%). Net shared savings to Medicare were $70.4 million (2021), $371.5 million (2022) and $694.6 million (2023), after the discount and high-performer bonuses; later years were not yet available. REACH ends after 2026 and is succeeded by the LEAD model in 2027.

summary: CMS reports progress toward its goal of every traditional Medicare beneficiary in an accountable care relationship by 2030. For 2026, MSSP's 12.6 million plus REACH's 1.7 million sums to about 14.3 million in these two programs. title: LEAD model: CMS's 10-year successor to ACO REACH
questions: What is the CMS LEAD model?
What replaces ACO REACH after 2026?
How does LEAD address the benchmark ratchet?
summary: CMS announced the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) model as the successor to ACO REACH, which ends after 2026. LEAD runs from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2036, which CMS calls the longest performance period it has tested. It offers a 10-year path to sustainable benchmarks without rebasing, a direct response to the ratchet complaints from ACOs, along with improved risk adjustment for high-needs patients. Participants choose Global risk (up to 100% of savings and losses) or Professional risk (up to 50%) and can receive capitated, population-based payments. CMS Administered Risk Arrangements (CARA) support episode-based arrangements between ACOs and specialists, and the model adds beneficiary cost-sharing support, a planned Part D premium buy-down by 2029, and a Medicaid partnership track for dual eligibles in two states. CMS aims to include smaller, independent and rural practices.

title: Milliman on ACO REACH PY2025 benchmark changes
questions: What changed in ACO REACH for 2025?
What is the ACO REACH regional blend cap?
How does ACO REACH handle coding intensity and V28?
summary: Milliman's September 2024 analysis summarizes CMS's PY2025 ACO REACH changes, most of which tighten benchmarks. For standard ACOs, the historical/regional blend stays at 55/45 rather than moving to 50/50, and the cap on upward regional adjustment drops from 5% to 3% of the adjusted FFS per capita cost; high-needs ACOs get a higher 9% ceiling. The Global benchmark discount stays at 3.5% for 2025, rising to 4.0% in 2026. Risk scores blend 33% of the V24 and 67% of the V28 CMS-HCC models, and the coding intensity factor is capped at 1%. Other changes cover voluntary alignment thresholds (500, or 250 for high-needs), a budget-neutral stop-loss multiplier, inclusion of GUIDE payments in expenditures, exclusion of two catheter codes tied to 2023 billing anomalies, and a revised area deprivation index for the health equity adjustment.

title: McKinsey (2022): VBC could reach ~$1 trillion in enterprise value (estimate)
questions: How big is the value-based care market?
What did McKinsey say about the value of value-based care companies?
Is value-based care a $1 trillion opportunity?
summary: McKinsey's 2022 article 'Investing in the new era of value-based care' argued that value-based care had become its own investable landscape. It estimated enterprise value of roughly $500 billion across payers, providers and enablers, potentially rising toward $1 trillion as the market matures, driven by lives in value-based arrangements growing 10-15% a year and lives in full or partial capitation growing faster (20-30%). It also projected the number of patients treated by physicians in value-based arrangements could roughly double over five years (about 15% annually), and noted investment in quality-over-volume companies rose more than 400% from 2019 to 2021. These are consulting projections, not measured market values, and later market events (MA rate pressure, provider retrenchment) have tested them. Secondary sources often attach a 2027 date, which the article does not clearly state.

title: Bain Frontline of Healthcare (2022): physicians want VBC but not much risk
questions: Do physicians want to participate in value-based care?
Are doctors ready for downside risk?
What do physicians say they need to succeed in VBC?
summary: Bain's November 2022 snap chart, drawn from its Frontline of Healthcare physician survey, found about 80% of physicians interested in value-based care arrangements, but interest falls as the provider's financial risk rises. Bain framed the core market problem as a mismatch: payers want cost savings and downside accountability, while many providers want upside-only deals, which has restrained VBC growth; two-sided models were under 20% of payments per HCP-LAN. Physicians reported feeling considerably less equipped to succeed in VBC than in Bain's 2017 and 2020 surveys, and said they needed more financial resources, better coding and billing processes, and more staff for reporting and outreach.

title: Bain (2023): most VBC dollars are upside-only; few physicians want full capitation
questions: How much healthcare spending is capitated?
What share of physicians want full capitation?
Do payers expect risk-based contracts to grow?
summary: At a June 2023 symposium, Bain presented a data view of the VBC market using 2021 payment data and its physician survey. Nearly 60% of 2021 payments had some link to quality or value, but nearly 40% had none; most value-linked dollars were upside-only, under 20% carried downside risk, and capitation was under 8% of spending. About 80% of physicians were interested in value-based arrangements, but only 13% were interested in full capitation, versus half interested in pay-for-performance. More than 80% of payers expected shared- and full-risk models to grow, with Medicare Advantage the fastest-growing segment. Deal volume and value had risen over five years but dipped in 2021-2022. These figures line up with HCP-LAN's 2021 data (40.5% pure fee-for-service, 19.6% downside risk, 7.4% Category 4).

title: HMA (2024): the crowded landscape of value-based enablers and risk-bearing entities
questions: What is a value-based care enabler?
How competitive is the VBC enablement market?
What are the risks of the value-based care enablement business model?
summary: Health Management Associates' January 2024 report studied about 120 value-based entities through secondary research and 60 interviews with entity leaders, providers and policymakers. It sorted them into three types: value-based payment enablers that help providers take on APMs without delivering care, risk-bearing delivery organizations, and hybrids. Most target the same providers, geographies and populations, pointing to a highly competitive market; most run high-touch hybrid clinical models with navigators, depend heavily on proprietary health IT, and rely on outside capital, with investor interest strong. Coverage spanned primary care and specialty areas tied to total-cost-of-care models such as kidney, oncology, cardiology, behavioral health and palliative care. HMA recommended guiding principles for entities and urged CMS to drive sustained provider participation and ensure high-quality partnerships.

summary: CMS has added equity-oriented features to MSSP. Advance Investment Payments (AIP) provide upfront payments to eligible ACOs. As of January 2025, 28 ACOs with 282,724 assigned beneficiaries received AIP; among those beneficiaries, 28% were Medicaid or LIS eligible, 9% lived in high-deprivation areas (ADI 85 or above) and 50% lived in health professional shortage or medically underserved areas. By January 2026, 36 ACOs covering 442,315 beneficiaries were in AIP, and a new Prepaid Shared Savings option had 4 ACOs with 51,005 beneficiaries. From 2025, benchmarks are also adjusted for the share of low-income assigned beneficiaries, and the quality scoring includes a health equity adjustment based on dual or LIS status and area deprivation. The program also counts 8,840 FQHCs and 3,109 RHCs as participants in 2026.

title: The ACO benchmark ratchet: what it is and the policy fixes on the table
questions: What is the ratchet effect in ACO benchmarks?
Why do successful ACOs leave MSSP?
What has CMS done to reduce the benchmark ratchet?
summary: The ratchet arises because MSSP rebases each new agreement period's benchmark on the ACO's own recent spending. An ACO that cuts spending lowers its future target, so continued success requires ever-deeper cuts, and the most efficient ACOs have the least room to earn savings. CMS has layered on partial mitigations: blending in regional spending, a prior-savings adjustment from 2024 that credits some past savings (with NAACOS noting a 5% cap on the prior savings and regional adjustments), eliminating the negative regional adjustment, and the fixed ACPT trend. NAACOS argues these are insufficient and has documented ACOs planning to exit. Proposed fixes include larger savings credits, removing the ACO's own beneficiaries from regional comparisons, and administrative benchmarks that do not rebase. CMS's LEAD model (2027-2036) promises a 10-year benchmark path without rebasing, the most direct test of a non-ratcheting design so far.
